newsitem.title: INDIA: India announces year's first sale of state assets.
newsitem.headline: India announces year's first sale of state assets.

text.p: The Indian government on Wednesday announced the first round of public asset sales for the year 1996-97 (April/March) as a step to bring its fiscal deficit to a targeted five percent of gross domestic product.
India said it will sell a seven percent stake in its external telecommunications firm Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd and five percent in its crude oil refining company Indian Oil Corporation.
The joint sale is expected to earn India around 15 billion rupees. The government is keen to raise at least 50 billion rupees before the current financial year ends in March 1997.
A government spokesman announced the plan to sell partial stakes in the two firms following a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.
Currently the government has an 82 percent stake in VSNL, the state-run agency which controls overseas telecommunications services in India.
The government has a 95 percent stake in IOC.
The spokesman said the shares could be sold in both domestic and overseas markets.
The spokesman said the exact prices of the two firms will be decided in consultations with merchant bankers to be appointed by the firms.
Analysts in India expect VSNL's share to be priced at around 1,350 rupees while IOC is expected to be offered at 750 rupees. The exat date for sale for shares is yet to be decided.

The government expects to raise another 35 billion rupees in two more tranches of sale of shares. These divestments will be done on the basis of recommendations made by a special panel appointed recently.
The panel is expected to examine about 240 state companies involved in various sectors including oil, telecommunication, steel, engineering and chemicals before before it recommends sale offers.
The government had targeted the sale of state shares as an important way to raise money for various items of expenditure as part of its economic reforms initiated in 1991.
However, depressed market conditions triggered mainly by poor money supply have often been an obstacle for smooth sale of shares in the past offers.

India could raise only around 3.6 billion rupees by sale of state shares in 1995-96 (April/March) against a projected 70 billion. India ended 1995-96 with an estimated fiscal deficit of 5.9 percent of is GDP.
